reason: The court itself held on appeal that R2, having been admitted without objection at trial, could not then be objected to.
The point was ratio, but the statement omits the material context that the duty was to specify the party and deadline for registering lis pendens under section 19(2)(b).
The judgment decided a belated lis pendens application in a partition action, not a general rule that parties must comply with statutory requirements by specified dates.
The delay in communicating the determination was material to overruling a delay objection in certiorari, but the statement drops that limiting procedural context.
The court relied on the natural-person/legal-person distinction to hold that a temple could not receive property as a fideicommissary.
The court held that references to temple property in the Buddhist Temporalities Ordinance concern sanghika property, which the disputed lands were not.
The trust argument was rejected because it was a mixed question of fact and law not raised in the District Court.
The proposition was part of the holding on an illegal tenancy, but it omits the no-certificate statutory illegality and cites section 13(2) instead of the provisions actually construed.
This was a fact-specific criticism supporting revision, not a legal holding, and the cited Civil Procedure Code provision was not the Code of Criminal Procedure provision construed.
The court found fraud on the particular police reports and facts, not a general legal rule about all public officials filing false reports, and the statute ID is wrong.
The covert-manoeuvre finding was a factual condemnation tied to the corrupt police assistance and null sale, while the statute ID does not match the provision construed.
The court's rule was that such an apparently absolute and irrevocable Kandyan gift could still be revoked, so this statement captures only the discarded premise.
The revocability holding is correct but materially omits the statutory qualification that the right is lost if expressly renounced in the required words.
The Roman-Dutch-law point is correct, but the statement drops the court's important qualification that connected matters such as revocability remain governed by Kandyan law.
The majority held, with Jameel J. dissenting, that children adopted under the Adoption of Children Ordinance could inherit from Muslim adopting parents on intestacy.
The rei vindicatio burden rule was the holding, but it was not a construction of section 3 of the Prescription Ordinance.
The co-owner point was ratio, but it omits the material warning that the decree will not bind absent co-owners and wrongly tags Civil Procedure Code section 18.
The burden rule was the court's holding, but it was a common-law boundary-action rule rather than a construction of Civil Procedure Code section 18.
The court held that title to Lot A could not be vindicated through a boundary action, but the claimed statute section was not the provision construed.
The distinction between lending money and carrying on the business of money lending was central to deciding the Money Lending Ordinance defence.
The statement is only an evidential observation about why a limited clientele did not help this plaintiff, not an independent holding.
The variety of securities was merely a factual indicator that this plaintiff was a professional money lender, not a rule of law.
The court used the statutory purpose of regulating house ownership as part of its construction of the tenant-purchase scheme.
The Bank-authority question was part of the holding, but the statement omits the two other statutory questions and the finality/judicial-review distinction.
The actual holding was that section 71(2) restrictions are jurisdictional and reviewable, not the vague proposition that the Finance Act restricts Bank acquisitions.
